ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All procedures were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Review Board (Protocol #17793).
Latino/Hispanic participants had the fewest group-specific markers (N = 3, "terrible", "find", "worse").
We initially recruited N = 1,798 adults via Prolific Academic between December 2025 and April 2026.

Eligibility criteria required current U.S. residency, age between 18 and 65, a minimum of 1,000 prior Prolific submissions, an approval rate of 95% or above, and self-identification as Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, Southeast Asian, Latino/Hispanic, or White.

To achieve racial/ethnic stratification, we used Prolific Academic's ethnicity filter to oversample Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, and Latino/Hispanic participants, supplemented by open recruitment for White participants.
Participants provided informed consent prior to enrollment.
Participants were compensated $5.00 upon completion of Session 1 (approximately 25 minutes) and $4.00 upon completion of Session 2 (approximately 5 minutes), for a total of $9.00.
At Session 1 (baseline), participants completed nine open-ended mental health prompts adapted from Hur et al. 38 (presented in randomized order), followed by the PHQ-8 and GAD-7.
table.formatted: At Session 1 (baseline), participants completed nine open-ended mental health prompts adapted from Hur et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> (presented in randomized order), followed by the PHQ-8 and GAD-7.

table.text: At Session 2, approximately three weeks later, participants completed the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 again.

At the baseline session, participants provided diary-style written responses to nine open-ended questions about their recent mental health experiences (e.g., "How has your energy been over the last two weeks?"

Retention rates differed significantly across racial/ethnic groups (χ²(3) = 15.60, p = .001): White participants had the highest retention (92.0%), followed by Black (87.4%), Asian (84.3%), and Latino/Hispanic (83.5%) participants.

FDR-corrected pairwise contrasts on race/ethnicity indicated that White participants were significantly more likely to complete Session 2 than Asian (OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.10, 3.89], p = .007) and Latino/Hispanic participants (OR = 2.20, 95% CI [1.19, 4.07], p = .004); the White-Black contrast did not survive correction (OR = 1.62, 95% CI [0.89, 2.94], p = .068).
Participants completed nine open-ended written prompts assessing recent mental health experiences at baseline, followed by the PHQ-8 (depression) and GAD-7 (generalized anxiety) self-report measures.
Approximately three weeks later, participants completed the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 again at Session 2 follow-up.
The sample was recruited via Prolific Academic and stratified by race/ethnicity.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori power analysis indicated that a minimum of N = 350 participants per racial/ethnic group would provide 80% power to detect an effect of r = 0.15 (α = .05). Therefore, we targeted 400 participants per group to account for attrition and data quality exclusions, yielding a recruitment goal of a minimum of 1,600 participants. To achieve racial/ethnic stratification, we used Prolific Academic's ethnicity filter to oversample Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, and Latino/Hispanic participants, supplemented by open recruitment for White participants. Of the 1,798 initially recruited, 113 were excluded from analyses for not completing the survey, either due to missing demographic data (N = 29), or for failing to self-identify within the four target racial/ethnic groups (N = 84). This ultimately produced a final sample of N = 1,685. Demographics by group are reported in Table 2. All procedures were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Review Board (Protocol #17793). Participants provided informed consent prior to enrollment. Participants were compensated $5.00 upon completion of Session 1 (approximately 25 minutes) and $4.00 upon completion of Session 2 (approximately 5 minutes), for a total of $9.00.

table.text: We-word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between We-word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.32, p = .267).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

table.header: Can machine-learning models predict psychopathology equivalently across groups?
table.expanded: In fact, a one-way ANOVA on participant-level absolute prediction errors (i.e., the absolute difference between predicted and self-reported symptom scores) revealed no significant difference across racial/ethnic groups (F(3, 1681) = 2.223, p = .084, ηp² = .004), indicating comparable model performance across groups.

table.formatted: Indeed, machine-learning models trained on baseline language also could not significantly predict follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were controlled for (all |Δr| ≤ .006, all p FDR ≥ .66; Table <ref type="table">S15</ref>).

table.formatted: Neither tone variable retained significant pairwise contrasts after correction (all ps > .11; Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>), but the omnibus interaction remained significant and the direction of differences were the same: For negative tone, the Latino/Hispanic slope was stronger than all others, and for positive tone, the Asian slope was stronger than all others (See Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).
table.expanded: Neither tone variable retained significant pairwise contrasts after correction (all ps > .11; Table S4), but the omnibus interaction remained significant and the direction of differences were the same: For negative tone, the Latino/Hispanic slope was stronger than all others, and for positive tone, the Asian slope was stronger than all others (See Table S3).
We-word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between We-word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.32, p = .267).
Social word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between social word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.40, p = .243).

The Cognitive Processing × race/ethnicity interaction term was not significant (F(3, 1662) = 0.22, p = .886), indicating no reliable evidence that the association between cognitive processing word usage and internalizing symptoms differs by race/ethnicity.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 16 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: A one-way ANOVA indicated that internalizing symptoms differed across racial groups (F(3, 1681) = 5.52, p < .001, ηp² = .01).
table.eta_coherence_note: Match under partial eta-squared formula from F and dfs.

table.text: A significant I-usage × race/ethnicity interaction emerged (F(3, 1662) = 3.48, p = .015), indicating that this association differed across groups.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: A significant negative tone × race/ethnicity interaction also emerged (F(3, 1662) = 3.28, p = .020; see Figure 2b), indicating that this association differed across groups.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: Similar to negative tone, a significant positive tone × race/ethnicity interaction was observed (F(3, 1662) = 5.00, p = .002; Figure 2c).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: First, we observed a significant interaction between race/ethnicity and the presence of the Physical Pain and Bodily Discomfort topic (F(3, 1662) = 6.31, p FDR < .001).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: The Depression Symptoms and Negative Affect topic, characterized by words like "gutted," "poorly," "bummer," "depressed," and "disappointed," also showed a significant race/ethnicity interaction (F(3, 1662) = 9.31, p FDR < .001).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: In fact, a one-way ANOVA on participant-level absolute prediction errors (i.e., the absolute difference between predicted and self-reported symptom scores) revealed no significant difference across racial/ethnic groups (F(3, 1681) = 2.223, p = .084, ηp² = .004), indicating comparable model performance across groups.
table.eta_coherence_note: Match under partial eta-squared formula from F and dfs.

table.text: We-word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between We-word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.32, p = .267).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: Social word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between social word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.40, p = .243).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: The Cognitive Processing × race/ethnicity interaction term was not significant (F(3, 1662) = 0.22, p = .886), indicating no reliable evidence that the association between cognitive processing word usage and internalizing symptoms differs by race/ethnicity.
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: Repeating these analyses on follow-up data showed that no LIWC language feature showed a significant race moderation when controlling for baseline symptoms: I-usage (F(3, 1441) = 0.26, p = .856), negative tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.89, p = .444), positive tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.69, p = .557), we-words (F(3, 1441) = 0.58, p = .630), social words (F(3, 1441) = 0.53, p = .661), and cognitive processing words (F(3, 1441) = 1.75, p = .155).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: Repeating these analyses on follow-up data showed that no LIWC language feature showed a significant race moderation when controlling for baseline symptoms: I-usage (F(3, 1441) = 0.26, p = .856), negative tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.89, p = .444), positive tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.69, p = .557), we-words (F(3, 1441) = 0.58, p = .630), social words (F(3, 1441) = 0.53, p = .661), and cognitive processing words (F(3, 1441) = 1.75, p = .155).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: In the pooled sample, adding language to baseline symptoms slightly reduced accuracy (r = .761 vs. .816; Δr = -.055, 95% CI [-.069, -.041]; t(1464) = -10.9, p < .001).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: We observed that racial/ethnic groups in our sample differed in mean baseline internalizing severity (PHQ-8 + GAD-7 composite; White M = 13.2, SD = 11.5; Black M = 11.4, SD = 11.4; Asian M = 12.6, SD = 11.7; Latino/Hispanic M = 14.5, SD = 12.65, F(3, 1681) = 5.52, p < .001).
table.eta_coherence_note: No parseable eta-squared effect size found.

table.text: A one-way ANOVA revealed no significant differences in absolute prediction errors across racial/ethnic groups (F(3, 1461) = 1.775, p = .150) indicating comparable prospective model performance across groups.

#### Data Files

#### Descriptives Overview

We found 31 columns with at least one missing value.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 2332 columns across 27 data files.
#### Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("LBA_topic_probabilities_with_outcomes.csv", "Shareable_for_zenodo.zip/Shareable/outputs/entropy_balancing/entropy_balanced_slopes_full_table.csv", "Shareable_for_zenodo.zip/Shareable/outputs/results/SI_slopes_entropy_balancing/entropy_balanced_slopes_full_table.csv", "followup_ML_error_ttests.csv", "followup_ML_error_ttests.csv" ), Column = c("user_id", "Race/Ethnicity", "Race/Ethnicity", "p", "p (FDR)"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: userid)", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\"/\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\"/\")", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 83% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"< ", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 83% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"< " )), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 27 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: All procedures were approved by the Princeton University Institutional Review Board (Protocol #17793).
live_data_statements: Latino/Hispanic participants had the fewest group-specific markers (N = 3, "terrible", "find", "worse").
We initially recruited N = 1,798 adults via Prolific Academic between December 2025 and April 2026.

Eligibility criteria required current U.S. residency, age between 18 and 65, a minimum of 1,000 prior Prolific submissions, an approval rate of 95% or above, and self-identification as Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, Southeast Asian, Latino/Hispanic, or White.

To achieve racial/ethnic stratification, we used Prolific Academic's ethnicity filter to oversample Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, and Latino/Hispanic participants, supplemented by open recruitment for White participants.
Participants provided informed consent prior to enrollment.
Participants were compensated $5.00 upon completion of Session 1 (approximately 25 minutes) and $4.00 upon completion of Session 2 (approximately 5 minutes), for a total of $9.00.
At Session 1 (baseline), participants completed nine open-ended mental health prompts adapted from Hur et al. 38 (presented in randomized order), followed by the PHQ-8 and GAD-7.
At Session 2, approximately three weeks later, participants completed the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 again.

At the baseline session, participants provided diary-style written responses to nine open-ended questions about their recent mental health experiences (e.g., "How has your energy been over the last two weeks?"

Retention rates differed significantly across racial/ethnic groups (χ²(3) = 15.60, p = .001): White participants had the highest retention (92.0%), followed by Black (87.4%), Asian (84.3%), and Latino/Hispanic (83.5%) participants.

FDR-corrected pairwise contrasts on race/ethnicity indicated that White participants were significantly more likely to complete Session 2 than Asian (OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.10, 3.89], p = .007) and Latino/Hispanic participants (OR = 2.20, 95% CI [1.19, 4.07], p = .004); the White-Black contrast did not survive correction (OR = 1.62, 95% CI [0.89, 2.94], p = .068).
Participants completed nine open-ended written prompts assessing recent mental health experiences at baseline, followed by the PHQ-8 (depression) and GAD-7 (generalized anxiety) self-report measures.
Approximately three weeks later, participants completed the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 again at Session 2 follow-up.
The sample was recruited via Prolific Academic and stratified by race/ethnicity.

#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 1 ran without error, 5 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `04_ngram_topic_analysis.R` after `04_ngram_topic_analysis.qmd`. **Undefined-variable errors**

**5 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. text.text: Psycholinguistic tools that estimate psychological symptoms from language alone aim to provide unobtrusive assessments without needing questionnaires or clinicians.
Researchers largely assume that these assessments function equivalently across demographic groups.

We tested this assumption in a racially diverse sample of U.S. adults (N = 1,685; Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, White) who described their mental health and completed standard symptom questionnaires.

Language-based markers of internalizing symptoms were often group-specific: First-person pronoun use predicted symptoms only among White participants, and sentiment varied in how strongly it tracked symptoms across groups.
Machine learning models trained on White participants' language produced higher prediction error for other groups than those groups' own models did.
Interpretability techniques revealed that White-trained models emphasized self-focused, agentic language more than minority groups' models.
These findings indicate that linguistic tools cannot assume generalizability and must be evaluated for the populations they serve.
We are in the midst of a mental health epidemic.
Nearly half of the U.S. population will experience a diagnosable psychological disorder in their lifetime 1 , and the prevalence of psychopathology continues to climb, despite all recent efforts 2 .
text.formatted: Nearly half of the U.S. population will experience a diagnosable psychological disorder in their lifetime <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> , and the prevalence of psychopathology continues to climb, despite all recent efforts <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Depression and anxiety diagnoses among U.S. adults have reached historic highs, rising fastest among Black and Latino/Hispanic adults 3 .
text.formatted: Depression and anxiety diagnoses among U.S. adults have reached historic highs, rising fastest among Black and Latino/Hispanic adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: However, access to psychological care has not kept pace with demand, as racial/ethnic minorities must often navigate both structural barriers (e.g., limited provider availability) and attitudinal barriers (e.g., stigma) to receive treatment 4 .
These same disparities extend to the severity and course of illness itself, as older Black and Latino/Hispanic adults show later onset but slower recovery from depression than White older adults 5.
text.formatted: These same disparities extend to the severity and course of illness itself, as older Black and Latino/Hispanic adults show later onset but slower recovery from depression than White older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref>.

text.text: One strategy for narrowing disparities in access to mental health care is to develop and disseminate tools that can identify people suffering from mental illness at scale without the added cost and infrastructure of in-clinic assessments.
To reach this broad aim, one promising approach has been to assess mental health through the words people use.
Language is at the core of psychological assessment and treatment [6] [7] [8] , and it is the natural medium through which people communicate their psychological states 9 .
text.formatted: Language is at the core of psychological assessment and treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> , and it is the natural medium through which people communicate their psychological states <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Thus, scholars are developing language-based assessments, or tools that analyze a person's natural language patterns to estimate their psychological well-being [10] [11] [12] .
text.formatted: Thus, scholars are developing language-based assessments, or tools that analyze a person's natural language patterns to estimate their psychological well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> .

text.text: Such tools can provide automatic and unobtrusive signals of a potential client's mental health needs or alert providers to a change in symptoms, all without additional burden to clients or the mental health care system.

Indeed, information theory suggests that open-ended responses can provide richer insight into psychological processes than asking clients to provide numerical ratings in response to questionnaire items 10, 13 .
text.formatted: Indeed, information theory suggests that open-ended responses can provide richer insight into psychological processes than asking clients to provide numerical ratings in response to questionnaire items <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: As a result, there is great enthusiasm for developing language-based assessments that improve both the validity and scalability of mental health measures.
A large body of work has shown that integrating computational linguistics with psychological theory can help craft tools that meaningfully assess psychopathology from language alone.

Using language from social media posts 14 , clinical interviews 15 , and even psychotherapy transcripts [16] [17] [18] [19] , these tools have been shown to predict symptoms of depression and anxiety with moderate-to-strong accuracy.
text.formatted: Using language from social media posts <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , clinical interviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> , and even psychotherapy transcripts <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> , these tools have been shown to predict symptoms of depression and anxiety with moderate-to-strong accuracy.

text.text: For example, a recent meta-analysis found a pooled accuracy of 80% for classifying depression from language in open-ended questions, clinical interviews, text messages, and therapeutic conversations 20 .
text.formatted: For example, a recent meta-analysis found a pooled accuracy of 80% for classifying depression from language in open-ended questions, clinical interviews, text messages, and therapeutic conversations <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: In particular, substantial evidence has identified first-person pronoun use (i.e., I-usage) and negative sentiment (i.e., the degree to which a text is positive or negative) as robust markers of depression across studies 17, 21, 22 .
text.formatted: In particular, substantial evidence has identified first-person pronoun use (i.e., I-usage) and negative sentiment (i.e., the degree to which a text is positive or negative) as robust markers of depression across studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: Theoretically, these associations are thought to reflect heightened self-focused attention and negative thoughts or beliefs 9, [23] [24] [25] , consistent with a broader body of work showing that depressed individuals hold more negative self-views than non-depressed individuals 26 .
text.formatted: Theoretically, these associations are thought to reflect heightened self-focused attention and negative thoughts or beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref> , consistent with a broader body of work showing that depressed individuals hold more negative self-views than non-depressed individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> .

text.text: Building on this line of work, recent large language model applications suggest that semantic representations of client "I" usage track within-and between-person differences in symptom severity across psychotherapy 27.
text.formatted: Building on this line of work, recent large language model applications suggest that semantic representations of client "I" usage track within-and between-person differences in symptom severity across psychotherapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref>.

text.text: However, most of this work estimates a stable relationship between language and psychological symptoms across all speakers, leaving open the possibility that this relationship varies across subgroups or with factors not yet considered.
Unfortunately, most studies modeling psychological symptoms do not examine if these relationships depend on demographic variables beyond age and gender 5 .
text.formatted: Unfortunately, most studies modeling psychological symptoms do not examine if these relationships depend on demographic variables beyond age and gender <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: Aguirre et al. 28 raised a parallel concern from a computational fairness perspective, warning that depression-detection models trained on social media language risk encoding demographic bias.
text.formatted: Aguirre et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> raised a parallel concern from a computational fairness perspective, warning that depression-detection models trained on social media language risk encoding demographic bias.

text.text: Indeed, Rai et al. 29 found that depression severity predicted greater I-usage and negative-emotion language among White social media users, but not Black users.
text.formatted: Indeed, Rai et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> found that depression severity predicted greater I-usage and negative-emotion language among White social media users, but not Black users.

text.text: They also found that machine learning models trained to predict depression from language performed well for White users but poorly for Black users, even when trained on Black users' own language.
One possible source of this lack of generalization is that the words people use to express distress vary across groups 30, 31 .
text.formatted: One possible source of this lack of generalization is that the words people use to express distress vary across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> .

text.text: Ramirez-Esparza et al. 32 , for instance, found that when Spanish-language forum users described their depression, they more often referenced relational concerns, whereas English-language users more frequently referenced medical concerns.
text.formatted: Ramirez-Esparza et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> , for instance, found that when Spanish-language forum users described their depression, they more often referenced relational concerns, whereas English-language users more frequently referenced medical concerns.

text.text: A body of work suggests that how people discuss psychological problems varies across cultures, races, and ethnicities.
In particular, minorities may be more likely to describe psychological distress through bodily or physical-related language, a pattern sometimes termed "somatization" 30, 33.
text.formatted: In particular, minorities may be more likely to describe psychological distress through bodily or physical-related language, a pattern sometimes termed "somatization" <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref>.

text.text: The findings of Rai et al. 29 challenge the assumptions that established linguistic markers behave similarly across racial and ethnic groups and that linguistic tools developed predominately on the language of one group can easily generalize to another.
text.formatted: The findings of Rai et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> challenge the assumptions that established linguistic markers behave similarly across racial and ethnic groups and that linguistic tools developed predominately on the language of one group can easily generalize to another.

text.text: If they do not, they risk either missing an individual's symptoms or overpathologizing them systematically based on their race or ethnicity.
This asymmetry presents a critical gap for both research and practice, as the people who might benefit most from these tools are also those they are least effective at serving.

Mental health assessment tools are not the first clinical tools to show variable performance across race: A widely used algorithm for identifying health risk was recently found to systematically underestimate the health needs of Black patients because of a race-confounded measure 34.
text.formatted: Mental health assessment tools are not the first clinical tools to show variable performance across race: A widely used algorithm for identifying health risk was recently found to systematically underestimate the health needs of Black patients because of a race-confounded measure <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref>.

text.text: Despite this concern, Rai et al. 29 remains the only study to have directly tested differences in language-based assessment performance across race.
text.formatted: Despite this concern, Rai et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> remains the only study to have directly tested differences in language-based assessment performance across race.

text.text: Here, we build on their findings through several key advances.

First, the prior study examined only Black and White groups, leaving open the question of whether these patterns extend to other racial and ethnic groups, including Latino/Hispanic and Asian populations, who together make up a large and growing share of the U.S. population 35 .
text.formatted: First, the prior study examined only Black and White groups, leaving open the question of whether these patterns extend to other racial and ethnic groups, including Latino/Hispanic and Asian populations, who together make up a large and growing share of the U.S. population <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> .

text.text: Second, they only analyzed language drawn from social media posts, raising the possibility that the observed pattern may reflect differences in how groups express themselves on social media, or the specific social-media-trained language model they used, rather than systematic differences in how depression manifests in language 36, 37 .
text.formatted: Second, they only analyzed language drawn from social media posts, raising the possibility that the observed pattern may reflect differences in how groups express themselves on social media, or the specific social-media-trained language model they used, rather than systematic differences in how depression manifests in language <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> .

text.text: Third, the study only examined a single timepoint, testing for contemporaneous associations between language and depression severity.
This leaves the open question of whether these group differences extend to prospective prediction.

Fourth, this and other studies typically do not report formal tests verifying that the criterion measures against which these tools are validated (i.e., symptom questionnaires) function equivalently across groups, an important foundation to establish before testing the generalizability of linguistic assessments of those very measures.
We sought to address these gaps in the current study.

Here, we perform a set of systematic tests examining whether the relationship between language and internalizing symptoms (i.e., anxiety and depression) generalize across racial and ethnic groups in a large, racially stratified online sample (N = 1,685; Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, and White adults).

At baseline, participants wrote responses to open-ended prompts about their recent mood, energy, and functioning, validated by previous research 38 (see Table 1), along with gold-standard questionnaire measures of anxiety and depression (Figure 1).
text.formatted: At baseline, participants wrote responses to open-ended prompts about their recent mood, energy, and functioning, validated by previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref>), along with gold-standard questionnaire measures of anxiety and depression (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Three weeks later, they completed the same measures again, allowing us to test both contemporaneous and prospective predictions of mental health symptoms with language.

Before testing for group differences, we confirmed that self-report measures of depression and anxiety functioned equivalently across groups, ensuring that observed differences reflected variation in symptoms rather than a measurement artifact.

We then asked: 1) whether established linguistic markers of psychopathology (e.g., first-person pronoun use, negative sentiment, and positive sentiment) predicted symptoms equally across racial and ethnic groups; 2) which specific words, phrases, and clusters of words (i.e., topics) characterized symptom severity within and across groups; and 3) whether machine learning models trained on one group's language predicted another group's symptoms as accurately as that group's own model; and 4) if not, which linguistic features the models weighted differently.
This work extends prior research 15, 21, 22, 25, 29 beyond simply asking whether language-based assessments predict psychopathology on average, to asking for whom they do so.
text.formatted: This work extends prior research <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> beyond simply asking whether language-based assessments predict psychopathology on average, to asking for whom they do so.

To ensure that any group differences we observed were not driven by the questionnaires themselves, we tested the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 for measurement invariance across racial/ethnic groups using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA).

Both scales showed full scalar invariance (PHQ-8: ΔCFI = .0003; GAD-7: ΔCFI = .0004; see Table S1), meaning that we can compare symptoms, and their relationship to language, across groups without differences in questionnaire function as a possible alternative explanation.

text.text: We next tested whether racial groups differed in the severity of their internalizing symptoms.
A one-way ANOVA indicated that internalizing symptoms differed across racial groups (F(3, 1681) = 5.52, p < .001, ηp² = .01).

text.text: Specifically, Latino/Hispanic participants reported significantly higher symptoms than Black participants (p Tukey < .001) with no other groups showing significant pairwise differences (M White = 13.2, M Black = 11.4, M Asian = 12.6, M Latino/Hispanic = 14.5, see Table S2 for pairwise comparison).

text.text: We tested whether key linguistic markers of internalizing symptoms identified in prior work (i.e., I-usage, and positive and negative sentiment) differed in their associations with symptoms across racial/ethnic groups.

Linguistic markers were computed using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC 41 ), a program that calculates the percentage of words in a text belonging to predefined psychological and linguistic categories (i.e., dictionaries).
text.formatted: Linguistic markers were computed using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> ), a program that calculates the percentage of words in a text belonging to predefined psychological and linguistic categories (i.e., dictionaries).

text.text: LIWC indexes sentiment through its positive tone and negative tone categories; we thus refer to these variable names when describing them in our analyses, and we use "sentiment" to refer to prior work.
For each marker, we estimated an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression model predicting baseline internalizing symptoms from each linguistic feature, race/ethnicity, and their interaction.
We also included demographic covariates (age, sex assigned at birth, and education level) in these models.
Language × race/ethnicity interaction terms were evaluated with an ANOVA using Type-III sums of squares.
Whenever this interaction was significant, we examined group-specific simple slopes and FDR-corrected slope contrasts (i.e., pairwise comparisons).

All analyses in the results section focus on contemporaneous associations between baseline language and baseline symptoms, except for the final section, which discusses prediction of follow-up symptom measures.
A significant I-usage × race/ethnicity interaction emerged (F(3, 1662) = 3.48, p = .015), indicating that this association differed across groups.
Replicating prior work, I-usage significantly predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants (β = 0.124, 95% CI [0.037, 0.211], p FDR = .021), controlling for age, sex, and education.

However, I-usage was not a significant predictor of internalizing symptoms for any racial minority group (i.e., Black, Asian, Latino participants; p FDR > .05; see Figure 2a; see Table S5 for full statistics).

text.text: FDR-adjusted pairwise contrasts confirmed that the slope for White participants was significantly steeper than the slopes for Black and Latino/Hispanic participants (p FDR < .05).

text.text: Together, these results indicate that I-usage functions as a marker of internalizing distress specifically among White participants.
A significant negative tone × race/ethnicity interaction also emerged (F(3, 1662) = 3.28, p = .020; see Figure 2b), indicating that this association differed across groups.

text.text: Together, these results indicate that negative tone tracks internalizing distress across all racial/ethnic groups, but this signal, in our sample, is amplified specifically among Latino/Hispanic participants.

text.text: Thus, higher positive tone tracks lower internalizing symptoms across all racial/ethnic groups, but this association was significantly weaker among Black participants relative to Asian and Latino/Hispanic participants.
Additional language variables.

We also examined a subset of other LIWC variables of theoretical interest (social words, we-words, and cognitive processing words) but found that none of these categories significantly interacted with race/ethnicity to track symptoms (p FDR > .2, see Figure S1a-c and Tables S7- S8 for full results).

text.text: Across groups, internalizing symptoms were associated with greater cognitive processing word usage, but symptoms were not significantly associated with social or we-word usage.
What are the linguistic patterns that characterized internalizing symptoms across and within racial groups?
We next used differential language analysis 42 to identify the words, phrases, and topics that correlated with internalizing symptom severity both across and within racial/ethnic groups.
text.formatted: We next used differential language analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> to identify the words, phrases, and topics that correlated with internalizing symptom severity both across and within racial/ethnic groups.

text.text: This technique differs from dictionary-based approaches, like LIWC, as it does not restrict analyses to a predefined word list.

We conducted two analyses: (1) an n-gram analysis identifying specific words and short phrases whose association with symptom severity varied by group, and (2) topic modeling, testing whether the frequency of semantically coherent language clusters ('topics') showed differential associations with internalizing symptoms across groups.
We identified all 1-to 3-word phrases (i.e., 1-to 3-grams) whose frequency was associated with internalizing symptom severity for each group.

This yielded a total of 59 n-grams that were significantly associated with internalizing symptoms within at least one group after FDR-correction and controlling for age, sex at birth, and education-level.

We then tested whether n-grams were associated with symptoms in each of our four racial/ethnic groups to identify which linguistic markers of distress were unique or shared across groups (see Figure 3; full statistics are presented in Table S9).
text.formatted: We then tested whether n-grams were associated with symptoms in each of our four racial/ethnic groups to identify which linguistic markers of distress were unique or shared across groups (see Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>; full statistics are presented in Table <ref type="table">S9</ref>).

text.text: Six (10%) n-grams showed significant associations with internalizing symptoms across all four groups.
These shared markers of distress included general psychological and evaluative terms (e.g., "low", "easier", "depressed", "exhausted", "good").

Another 13 (22%) n-grams were significantly associated with internalizing symptoms in two or three racial/ethnic groups, representing common signals of psychopathology that cut across group boundaries.
These shared markers spanned both affective and evaluative language.

Terms reflecting explicit negative affect and clinical distress ( "sad", "anxious". "anxiety", "depression", and "failure") were shared across multiple groups, as were evaluative terms describing life satisfaction ("dissatisfied", "satisfied", "poor") and general difficulty ("hard", "difficult").

Notably, several shared markers were negatively associated with internalizing symptoms, indicating that use of positively valenced terms such as "happy", "satisfied", and "higher" were associated with less distress across groups.
The remaining 40 n-grams (68%) were significantly associated with symptoms in only a single group, and their semantic content differed substantially across groups.
Black participants showed the largest set of group-specific markers (N = 15), featuring somatic and physical language alongside affective terms (e.g., "pain", "weak", "stomach", "angry").
White participants' 14 group-specific markers centered on chronicity and cognitive framing (e.g., "chronic", "never", "hopeless" ).
Asian participants' 8 group-specific markers emphasized temporal and mood-tracking language (e.g., "mood_lower_usual", "couple weeks").
Latino/Hispanic participants had the fewest group-specific markers (N = 3, "terrible", "find", "worse").

text.text: We then tested whether the use of words within "topics" (i.e., groups of words shown to cluster into semantic themes) showed differential associations with internalizing symptoms across race/ethnicity groups.
We selected and tested 54 of 2,000 topics drawn from a pretrained model developed by past researchers 42 .
text.formatted: We selected and tested 54 of 2,000 topics drawn from a pretrained model developed by past researchers <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> .

text.text: Twenty-two topics showed significant main effects on internalizing symptoms after correction (p FDR < .05), spanning constructs including depression, romantic loss, chronic illness, and physical pain.
text.formatted: Twenty-two topics showed significant main effects on internalizing symptoms after correction (p FDR < .05), spanning constructs including depression, romantic loss, chronic illness, and physical pain.

text.text: However, only two topics showed significant interactions with race/ethnicity in predicting internalizing symptoms (p FDR < .05; see Figure 4).

text.text: First, we observed a significant interaction between race/ethnicity and the presence of the Physical Pain and Bodily Discomfort topic (F(3, 1662) = 6.31, p FDR < .001).

text.text: Together, these results indicate that somatic language carries a stronger signal of internalizing distress among racial/ethnic minority groups than among White participants, consistent with prior work documenting different norms linking somatic symptom expression to psychological disclosures across racial/ethnic groups.

The Depression Symptoms and Negative Affect topic, characterized by words like "gutted," "poorly," "bummer," "depressed," and "disappointed," also showed a significant race/ethnicity interaction (F(3, 1662) = 9.31, p FDR < .001).

Slopes did not differ significantly among White, Black, and Latino/Hispanic participants (all p FDR > .05; see Table S11 for full contrast statistics).

text.text: Thus, this cluster of affective language is a less reliable marker of internalizing severity among Asian participants, which may reflect cultural differences in the directness of emotional expression.
The analyses above relied on word frequency, which do not account for the context in which words are used.
Word embeddings resolve this issue by representing text in a high-dimensional space organized around meaning.
Machine-learning (i.e., ridge regression) models can learn to predict symptoms based on word embeddings with high accuracy 10 .
text.formatted: Machine-learning (i.e., ridge regression) models can learn to predict symptoms based on word embeddings with high accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: We next tested whether such approaches could predict internalizing symptoms in our sample and whether these models performed equivalently across racial/ethnic groups.
Within-group performance.

We generated contextual word embeddings for each participant's language using MentalRoBERTa, and used these embeddings as features in a ridge regression model to predict internalizing symptoms with 5-fold cross validation.
Results showed our model predicted internalizing symptoms from participants' written text with strong accuracy across the full sample (r = 0.738, 95% CI [0.719, 1], p < .001).
text.formatted: Results showed our model predicted internalizing symptoms from participants' written text with strong accuracy across the full sample (r = 0.738, 95% CI [0.719, 1], p < .001).

text.text: We next built four group-specific models, each trained and evaluated on text within each racial group using 5-fold cross-validation with a fixed penalty.

We found that each model performed well in predicting internalizing symptoms within the same racial group: White (r = 0.708, 95% CI [0.665, 1,] p < .001), Black (r = 0.690, 95% CI [0.657, 1], p < .001), Asian (r = 0.753, 95% CI [0.713, 1], p < .001), and Latino/Hispanic (r = 0.742, 95% CI [0.701, 1], p < .001).
text.formatted: We found that each model performed well in predicting internalizing symptoms within the same racial group: White (r = 0.708, 95% CI [0.665, 1,] p < .001), Black (r = 0.690, 95% CI [0.657, 1], p < .001), Asian (r = 0.753, 95% CI [0.713, 1], p < .001), and Latino/Hispanic (r = 0.742, 95% CI [0.701, 1], p < .001).

text.text: In fact, a one-way ANOVA on participant-level absolute prediction errors (i.e., the absolute difference between predicted and self-reported symptom scores) revealed no significant difference across racial/ethnic groups (F(3, 1681) = 2.223, p = .084, ηp² = .004), indicating comparable model performance across groups.
Comparing within-group and across-group predictions.

Next, we examined how well models trained on one racial/ethnic group's language data generalized to unseen data from another group by computing the difference in error for across-group predictions vs. that target group's own in-group model (see Figure 5 and Methods for details).
text.formatted: Next, we examined how well models trained on one racial/ethnic group's language data generalized to unseen data from another group by computing the difference in error for across-group predictions vs. that target group's own in-group model (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">5</ref> and Methods for details).

text.text: We found that the White-trained model produced significantly higher error predicting internalizing symptoms for Black, Latino/Hispanic, and Asian participants than each of those groups' own models produced (p FDR < .001; see Table S12 for full statistics).
text.formatted: We found that the White-trained model produced significantly higher error predicting internalizing symptoms for Black, Latino/Hispanic, and Asian participants than each of those groups' own models produced (p FDR < .001; see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S12</ref> for full statistics).

text.text: Minority-trained models showed a more differentiated pattern.
The Black-trained model produced significantly higher error for Asian participants than the Asian model did (p FDR = .002).

By contrast, the Latino/Hispanic-and Asian-trained models produced significantly lower error on White participants' text than the White model produced on its own group (p FDR 's = .015 and .002 respectively).
Across all 12 pairings, the White-trained model was the only one with significantly higher error than the target group's own model for all three other groups.
Each minority-trained model, by contrast, showed higher error for zero or one other group.
To better understand why the models differed, we examined how each group's model weighted language when estimating symptom severity.
Each model learned a vector in embedding space that points from low-to high-severity language.

The cosine similarity of these vectors (a measure of how closely two vectors align;1 = identical,0 = unrelated) ranged from 0.796 to 0.891 (see Table S13), indicating that all groups' models learned broadly similar, but not identical, patterns to gauge severity.
text.formatted: The cosine similarity of these vectors (a measure of how closely two vectors align;1 = identical,0 = unrelated) ranged from 0.796 to 0.891 (see Table <ref type="table">S13</ref>), indicating that all groups' models learned broadly similar, but not identical, patterns to gauge severity.

text.text: Interestingly, the three minority groups' severity vectors were more similar to one another (mean pairwise cosine similarity = 0.847) than to the White model's (mean = 0.807).
This parallels the results above, in which the White-trained model was the only one with higher error on every other group.

Thus, for the word-level analyses that follow, we collapse the three minority-group vectors into a single mean minority-group vector for the primary comparison reported below (see Figure S2 for analyses of each minority model).

text.text: We then computed a vector that captures the difference in what the White-model vs. minority-model had learned to associate with symptoms, and we projected words onto this difference vector, which shows how much that word contributes to a given model's severity predictions 43 .

text.text: Figure 6 shows, for each displayed word, the difference between the two models: how much more strongly one model links that word to high severity than the other does.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">6</ref> shows, for each displayed word, the difference between the two models: how much more strongly one model links that word to high severity than the other does.

text.text: Words at the extremes are therefore the ones on which the two models disagree most.
This analysis showed that the two models learned to associate different words with internalizing symptoms.

Compared to the minority-group model, the White model linked high severity more strongly with agentic, self-focused, and goal-directed language including words like: "myself", "goals", "self", "motivated", "focus", "concentration", and "decision" alongside engagement and interest-related language such as "interest," "hobbies", "enjoy", "reading", and "activities."

The minority-group model, by contrast, was dominated by temporal and seasonal language, with "earlier", "holidays", "cold", "lately", "weather", "later", "morning", "early", and "nights" among the words most strongly weighted toward severity.

This suggests that whereas the White model's severity direction relied more on self-referential, motivational, and interest-based content, the minority-group model's severity direction relied more on temporal framing, such as references to time of day, recency, and seasonal or holiday context.

A secondary pattern also emerged for the minority-group model around describing functional change ("harder", "easier", "better", "different", "bad", "fine"), suggesting relatively greater sensitivity to language describing change relative to a prior baseline.

Analyses of each minority racial/ethnic group's model against the White model showed similar patterns to this overall contrast (see Figure S2). severity between the White model and the combined minority models (Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic averaged together).

The x-axis shows how much more strongly one model weights that word toward severity, with larger absolute values indicating greater disagreement between groups in how strongly that word signals severity.
All models were fit with matched hyperparameters (λ = 250) so that differences in the learned weights are not attributable to differences in regularization.
The figure shows the 20 words at each end of the distribution of weight differences.

We designed this study to allow us to examine whether the ability to predict follow-up symptoms assessed three weeks later based on baseline language (as in Hur et al. 38 ) also differed across races (see Tables S14-16).

text.text: None of the LIWC variables predicted follow-up symptoms after controlling for baseline symptoms, and none showed moderation by race (see Supplemental Information).
These null predictions may be due to the fact that symptoms were highly stable across the three-week period (r = .817, 95% CI [.799, .833], p < .001).
text.formatted: These null predictions may be due to the fact that symptoms were highly stable across the three-week period (r = .817, 95% CI [.799, .833], p < .001).

text.text: Indeed, machine-learning models trained on baseline language also could not significantly predict follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were controlled for (all |Δr| ≤ .006, all p FDR ≥ .66; Table S15).
text.formatted: Indeed, machine-learning models trained on baseline language also could not significantly predict follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were controlled for (all |Δr| ≤ .006, all p FDR ≥ .66; Table <ref type="table">S15</ref>).

text.text: These machine-learning models controlling for baseline symptoms also showed no cross-group differences in prediction accuracy (all p FDR ≥ .85; Table S16).
text.formatted: These machine-learning models controlling for baseline symptoms also showed no cross-group differences in prediction accuracy (all p FDR ≥ .85; Table <ref type="table">S16</ref>).

text.text: Interestingly, though, machine learning models trained on baseline language did predict follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were not controlled for (r pooled = 0.565, 95%CI [0.535, 1], p < .001), and the cross-group asymmetry in predictive accuracy was still present:
text.formatted: Interestingly, though, machine learning models trained on baseline language did predict follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were not controlled for (r pooled = 0.565, 95%CI [0.535, 1], p < .001), and the cross-group asymmetry in predictive accuracy was still present:

text.text: The White-trained model again produced significantly higher error for all three minority groups than each group's own model did in predicting follow-up symptoms (Table S14; Figure S3).
text.formatted: The White-trained model again produced significantly higher error for all three minority groups than each group's own model did in predicting follow-up symptoms (Table <ref type="table">S14</ref>; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">S3</ref>).

text.text: Thus, racial differences in the accuracy of language-based estimates are not confined to a single timepoint and persist to symptom reports three weeks later, but neither LIWC features nor these machine learning models predicted change in symptoms when baseline symptoms are controlled for.

Language-based assessments are increasingly proposed as scalable, low-burden supplements to closed-ended symptom scales, and a growing body of work shows they can index psychological health with remarkable accuracy 16, 44, 45 .
text.formatted: Language-based assessments are increasingly proposed as scalable, low-burden supplements to closed-ended symptom scales, and a growing body of work shows they can index psychological health with remarkable accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> .

text.text: However, the utility of these measures rests on an assumption that the associations between language and symptoms are the same regardless of who is producing that language.
Here we extend initial evidence challenging this assumption 29 using three complementary language analyses in a large, racially stratified sample of U.S. adults spanning four racial/ethnic groups.
text.formatted: Here we extend initial evidence challenging this assumption <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> using three complementary language analyses in a large, racially stratified sample of U.S. adults spanning four racial/ethnic groups.

text.text: We found that first-person singular pronoun use, a well-established marker of depression 21, 22, 25 , predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants but not Black, Asian, or Latino/Hispanic participants.
text.formatted: We found that first-person singular pronoun use, a well-established marker of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> , predicted internalizing symptoms among White participants but not Black, Asian, or Latino/Hispanic participants.

text.text: Associations between symptoms and sentiment markers also differed across groups: Negative sentiment was more strongly linked to symptoms for Latino than White participants and positive sentiment was more strongly linked for Latino than Black participants.
A differential language analysis recovered a core set of words and phrases that characterized symptoms across all four groups, along with phrases and topics that were group-specific.
Interestingly, somatic language carried a stronger signal of distress among minority groups than among White participants.
Machine learning models trained within each group predicted symptoms accurately for that group.

However, they did not transfer equivalently when deployed out-of-group; the White-trained model produced significantly higher error for all three racial/ethnic minority groups than those groups' own models did.
Finally, an interpretive technique linking model predictions back to individual words revealed that the White model weighted self-focused, agentic language more heavily than minority models.
These findings suggest language-based tools cannot assume uniform validity and must be evaluated for the populations they serve.

Like Rai et al. 29 , we found that I-usage predicted depression severity among White but not Black participants, and that a model trained on White participants' language produced higher error for Black participants than a model trained on Black participants' own language did.
text.formatted: Like Rai et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> , we found that I-usage predicted depression severity among White but not Black participants, and that a model trained on White participants' language produced higher error for Black participants than a model trained on Black participants' own language did.

text.text: Here, we extend this result in several ways.
First, we demonstrated that the pattern was not confined to the Black-White comparison, as I-usage also did not predict symptoms among Latino/Hispanic participants or Asian participants.
Second, we found that other language markers showed more nuanced patterns of associations with symptoms across groups.
Sentiment (i.e., the positivity or negativity of language) predicted internalizing symptoms in all four groups.
However, the association for negative sentiment was stronger among Latino/Hispanic than White participants.
Thus, it does not appear that language-based assessments perform uniformly across minority groups.
Instead, different linguistic features may over or underestimate symptoms, depending on the racial group.
Third, we showed that this effect emerges outside of social media platforms.

Many prior demonstrations of language features predicting mental illness from language have relied on social media text 14, 28, 29, 46 , raising the possibility that platform-specific disclosure norms 36,37   , rather than differences in expression, could help to explain the observed effects.
text.formatted: Many prior demonstrations of language features predicting mental illness from language have relied on social media text <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> , raising the possibility that platform-specific disclosure norms 36,37   , rather than differences in expression, could help to explain the observed effects.

text.text: We fixed the disclosure context across groups by analyzing participants' responses to prompts validated by prior research 38 .
text.formatted: We fixed the disclosure context across groups by analyzing participants' responses to prompts validated by prior research <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> .

text.text: This helped minimize concerns about group differences emerging due to norms for how distress is expressed on various platforms.
An additional goal was to test whether these group differences in language-symptom associations extend to the prospective prediction of symptom change.

LIWC-based markers did not significantly predict follow-up symptoms in any group after controlling for baseline severity, likely because symptoms were highly stable across the three-week assessment window, leaving little residual variance for these features to explain (see Supplemental Information).
We also found that machine learning models did not transfer equally across training and test groups.
Across all twelve model-group pairings, the White-trained model was the only one to produce significantly higher error than every other group's own in-group model.
By contrast, the Asian-and Latino/Hispanic-trained models each produced significantly lower prediction error for White participants than the White model produced on its own group.
This pattern argues against an obvious alternative explanation that minority-group models performed worse because they were trained on less data and were therefore noisier.
If that were the case, the minority-trained models, not the White-trained model, should have generalized poorly to other groups.
Instead, it seems that the content each model learns to associate with symptoms is more similar for minority-trained models than the White-trained model.

Indeed, although the four groups' learned severity directions were broadly similar, with pairwise cosine similarities ranging from .796 to .891, they differed in what words they weighted to be aligned with higher internalizing symptoms.
The White model's severity direction was anchored in agentic, self-referential, and motivational content, aligning with cognitive theories of depression 23, 47, 48 .
text.formatted: The White model's severity direction was anchored in agentic, self-referential, and motivational content, aligning with cognitive theories of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48</ref> .

text.text: The minority-mean direction was anchored instead in temporal and seasonal framing, alongside language describing functional change relative to a prior baseline.
This suggests that the White model weighs some linguistic features differently from those most informative for these groups, which could contribute to its higher cross-group prediction error.
This asymmetry also held when models trained on baseline language predicted symptoms three weeks later.
However, because symptoms were highly stable, this prospective prediction was eliminated once baseline symptoms were included.
Thus, the higher cross-group error persists when predicting symptom scores at a later timepoint (but not when predicting changes in those scores relative to baseline).
Similarly, our differential language analyses showed that somatic and physical language carried a stronger signal of internalizing symptoms among minority groups than among White participants.

This pattern emerged both in topic modeling and n-gram analyses where the physical pain topic and phrases like "stomach," "terrible," and "pain" were only associated with symptoms for minority participants.
This pattern aligns with prior arguments that Black and Latino/Hispanic groups talk about mental health concerns in terms of somatic issues 30, 33 , though see 49, 50 for contrasting views.
text.formatted: This pattern aligns with prior arguments that Black and Latino/Hispanic groups talk about mental health concerns in terms of somatic issues <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> , though see <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50</ref> for contrasting views.

text.text: Other results were also consistent with past research.
In particular, the Depression Symptoms and Negative Affect topic was a weaker marker of symptoms for Asian participants than other groups.

This is in line with research that shows individuals of Asian heritage often suppress emotions more than their European-American counterparts, and that the link between suppression and depressive symptoms is attenuated for Asian individuals 51 .
text.formatted: This is in line with research that shows individuals of Asian heritage often suppress emotions more than their European-American counterparts, and that the link between suppression and depressive symptoms is attenuated for Asian individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">51</ref> .

text.text: As a result, language sentiment may therefore be a weaker indicator of psychological distress for Asian individuals.

These findings highlight the power of language-based analyses to uncover relevant psychological constructs and prompt further research on the psychological and linguistic patterns that index pathology in each group 10, 52.
text.formatted: These findings highlight the power of language-based analyses to uncover relevant psychological constructs and prompt further research on the psychological and linguistic patterns that index pathology in each group <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref>.

text.text: A key question for our findings is whether they reflect actual differences in how distress is expressed across groups or instead artifacts of measurement, sampling, or context.
Several aspects of our design allow us to speak against some of the most plausible alternative explanations.

First, our mental health measures showed comparable functioning across groups, which reduces the likelihood that differences in language-symptom associations reflect differences in how the symptom measures themselves behaved.
Second, although racial/ethnic groups differed in mean baseline symptom severity, effects that paralleled these differences were robust when we equated groups on severity with entropy balancing.
Third, as discussed above, scholars have raised the concern that platform-specific disclosure norms 36, 37 , rather than differences in expression, may motivate the observed effects.
text.formatted: Third, as discussed above, scholars have raised the concern that platform-specific disclosure norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> , rather than differences in expression, may motivate the observed effects.

text.text: However, we fixed the disclosure context across groups by analyzing responses to the same prompts validated by prior research 38 , so such norms are unlikely to serve as explanations for our findings.
text.formatted: However, we fixed the disclosure context across groups by analyzing responses to the same prompts validated by prior research <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> , so such norms are unlikely to serve as explanations for our findings.

text.text: Finally, an overlapping constellation of results emerged across three different analytic approaches: a dictionary-based program 41 , n-gram and topic analyses 42, 53 , and machine learning models trained on word embeddings 54, 55 , suggesting these differences reflect a property of the language-symptom relationship rather than an artifact of any particular method.
text.formatted: Finally, an overlapping constellation of results emerged across three different analytic approaches: a dictionary-based program <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> , n-gram and topic analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> , and machine learning models trained on word embeddings <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> , suggesting these differences reflect a property of the language-symptom relationship rather than an artifact of any particular method.

text.text: Our work has several implications for language-based mental health research.

Most importantly, our results caution against treating language-based assessment models as validated once they produce acceptable pooled accuracy benchmarks, a practice that is increasingly common as digital mental health platforms adopt language-based screening at scale 45, 56 .
text.formatted: Most importantly, our results caution against treating language-based assessment models as validated once they produce acceptable pooled accuracy benchmarks, a practice that is increasingly common as digital mental health platforms adopt language-based screening at scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56</ref> .

text.text: The higher cross-group prediction error we observed suggests that a model trained predominantly on one group's language (as many existing tools often are, given the demographic composition of social media and clinical training corpora) 57, 58 , could systematically under or over-estimate symptom severity for the very populations facing the greatest structural barriers to traditional care.
text.formatted: The higher cross-group prediction error we observed suggests that a model trained predominantly on one group's language (as many existing tools often are, given the demographic composition of social media and clinical training corpora) <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58</ref> , could systematically under or over-estimate symptom severity for the very populations facing the greatest structural barriers to traditional care.

text.text: This difference would carry little to no signal in aggregated performance metrics, such that a tool could appear validated while producing less accurate estimates for the populations it most needs to reach.

In fact, this presents a critical gap for platforms already deploying language-based screening at scale, echoing the pitfalls of the "one-size-fits-most" approach documented in other clinical algorithms 34 .
text.formatted: In fact, this presents a critical gap for platforms already deploying language-based screening at scale, echoing the pitfalls of the "one-size-fits-most" approach documented in other clinical algorithms <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref> .

text.text: This concern is not new to psychometrics, as research has documented that both clinical and educational instruments can function differently across demographics, and ignoring these differences can perpetuate structural inequalities 59, 60 .
text.formatted: This concern is not new to psychometrics, as research has documented that both clinical and educational instruments can function differently across demographics, and ignoring these differences can perpetuate structural inequalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">60</ref> .

text.text: Longer-term, our findings point toward a more targeted solution where model developers audit which specific features drive predictions for a given population and reweight or retrain accordingly.
Achieving this kind of targeted, population-sensitive validation is unlikely to happen within a siloed field.

It will require sustained collaboration between people like the computer scientists who build these models, clinicians and cultural psychologists who understand how distress is expressed across groups [61] [62] [63] , and more importantly the communities these tools are meant to serve.
text.formatted: It will require sustained collaboration between people like the computer scientists who build these models, clinicians and cultural psychologists who understand how distress is expressed across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[62]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[63]</ref> , and more importantly the communities these tools are meant to serve.

text.text: Although the use of a large racially stratified sample, validated prompts, and convergence across diverse analytic methods are strengths of the current research, several limitations should be addressed by future work.

Most importantly, individual difference measures like race and ethnicity are often coarse measurements of the underlying processes that shape language use, including emotion socialization, cultural context, acculturation, and lived experiences 32, 61, 62, 64 .
text.formatted: Most importantly, individual difference measures like race and ethnicity are often coarse measurements of the underlying processes that shape language use, including emotion socialization, cultural context, acculturation, and lived experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">61,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">62,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">64</ref> .

text.text: Although we document variation across these broad social categories, future work should identify the underlying psychological and cultural processes that drive these differences.
Our four-group design also collapsed distinctions that are likely to matter, including those across East, South, and Southeast Asian participants.
This precludes us from testing differences in acculturation, generational status, or language background.

Identifying which processes motivate these differences, such as help-seeking norms 4 , or other social features, requires measuring them directly rather than inferring them from group membership alone.
text.formatted: Identifying which processes motivate these differences, such as help-seeking norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> , or other social features, requires measuring them directly rather than inferring them from group membership alone.

text.text: Additionally, our sample was recruited online, resided in the United States, wrote in English, and spanned a largely subclinical to moderate range of symptom severity.

This presents a rich open set of questions for future research around whether these patterns hold in clinical populations, in other languages or cultures, and whether illness severity modulates these associations.
Language-based assessments hold considerable promise for expanding access to mental health screening at scale, without the added cost or clinical infrastructure traditional assessment requires.
However, to deploy them effectively, we must address the differences in cross-group accuracy that we found here.

These findings provide further evidence that the validity of language-based assessments must be established on populations they are intended to serve, rather than assumed from average performance in pooled samples.
However, doing so is possible with existing tools, and careful attention to the linguistic signals of distress used by diverse groups can also guide psychological theory and discovery.

Our central hypothesis, that language-symptom associations vary by race/ethnicity, was generated prior to launching the study, inspired by Rai et al. 29 .
