text.text: We extended their methods and analytic approach to four racial/ethnic groups and added two additional methods: n-gram analysis and embedding projections.

The specific words, phrases, and topics these methods identified were not preregistered, given that open-vocabulary and embedding-based methods surface patterns from the data rather than testing a predefined list.

Lastly, given the number of analyses we report, we applied an FDR-correction 66 within each analysis family (e.g., across a given LIWC variable's pairwise group contrasts, across all candidate n-grams within a group, across all 54 candidate topics, across machine learning model comparisons) to reduce inflated error from multiple comparisons.

text.text: We initially recruited N = 1,798 adults via Prolific Academic between December 2025 and April 2026.

Eligibility criteria required current U.S. residency, age between 18 and 65, a minimum of 1,000 prior Prolific submissions, an approval rate of 95% or above, and self-identification as Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, Southeast Asian, Latino/Hispanic, or White.
An a priori power analysis indicated that a minimum of N = 350 participants per racial/ethnic group would provide 80% power to detect an effect of r = 0.15 (α = .05).
Therefore, we targeted 400 participants per group to account for attrition and data quality exclusions, yielding a recruitment goal of a minimum of 1,600 participants.

To achieve racial/ethnic stratification, we used Prolific Academic's ethnicity filter to oversample Black/African American, East Asian, South Asian, and Latino/Hispanic participants, supplemented by open recruitment for White participants.

Of the 1,798 initially recruited, 113 were excluded from analyses for not completing the survey, either due to missing demographic data (N = 29), or for failing to self-identify within the four target racial/ethnic groups (N = 84).
This ultimately produced a final sample of N = 1,685.

At Session 1 (baseline), participants completed nine open-ended mental health prompts adapted from Hur et al. 38 (presented in randomized order), followed by the PHQ-8 and GAD-7.

text.text: Using LIWC variables, we found no significant prospective associations between baseline language and follow-up symptoms after controlling for baseline symptom severity.
Accordingly, all LIWC results reported in the main text reflect contemporaneous associations between language and symptoms; we report the prospective LIWC analyses in the Supplemental Information.
Machine learning models significantly predicted follow-up symptoms when baseline symptoms were not included, but not after controlling for baseline symptoms.
We summarize these results in the main text and report full statistics in the Supplemental Information.
Open-Ended Mental Health Prompts.

At the baseline session, participants provided diary-style written responses to nine open-ended questions about their recent mental health experiences (e.g., "How has your energy been over the last two weeks?"
; adapted from prior work 38 ) and presented in randomized order.
text.formatted: ; adapted from prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> ) and presented in randomized order.

text.text: Prompts were designed to map onto core symptom domains of depression and anxiety (see Table 1 for full prompt list).
text.formatted: Prompts were designed to map onto core symptom domains of depression and anxiety (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref> for full prompt list).

text.text: Responses across all nine prompts were concatenated into a single text per participant, which was used for all language analyses.
Self-Report Measures.

Depressive symptom severity was assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8) 68 , and generalized anxiety symptom severity was assessed using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) 69 .
text.formatted: Depressive symptom severity was assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-8 (PHQ-8) <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">68</ref> , and generalized anxiety symptom severity was assessed using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">69</ref> .

text.text: Both scales demonstrated excellent internal consistency in our sample, with reliability consistent across racial/ethnic groups: PHQ-8: α = .915 overall (Asian = .920, Black = .909, Latino/Hispanic = .918, White = .914); GAD-7: α = .937 overall (Asian = .941, Black = .933, Latino/Hispanic = .941, White = .932).

PHQ-8 and GAD-7 baseline scores were highly correlated (r = 0.84, 95% CI [0.83, 0.86], p < .001), consistent with the high comorbidity of depression and anxiety and the shared internalizing factor structure 70 .
text.formatted: PHQ-8 and GAD-7 baseline scores were highly correlated (r = 0.84, 95% CI [0.83, 0.86], p < .001), consistent with the high comorbidity of depression and anxiety and the shared internalizing factor structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">70</ref> .

text.text: Accordingly, as in prior work [16] [17] [18] [19] , we computed an internalizing composite by summing PHQ-8 and GAD-7 scores (range: 0-45), which served as the primary outcome for all analyses.
text.formatted: Accordingly, as in prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> , we computed an internalizing composite by summing PHQ-8 and GAD-7 scores (range: 0-45), which served as the primary outcome for all analyses.

text.text: Do self-report depression and anxiety measures behave similarly across racial groups?

Before comparing PHQ-8 and GAD-7 scores across racial/ethnic groups, we first verified that both scales measured depression and anxiety similarly across groups, a prerequisite for valid group comparisons.

If a scale functions differently across groups (e.g., if the same response reflects different levels of distress for different people), then observed score differences could reflect measurement artifacts rather than true differences in symptoms.
We tested this using MGCFA, a statistical approach that examines whether a questionnaire's underlying structure holds equally across groups 71 .
text.formatted: We tested this using MGCFA, a statistical approach that examines whether a questionnaire's underlying structure holds equally across groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">71</ref> .

text.text: We tested three levels of equivalence in sequence.
First, we asked whether the same items cluster together into the same factor across groups (configural invariance).
Second, we asked whether each item was equally strongly related to the underlying construct across groups (metric invariance).
Third, we asked whether participants from different groups who endorse the same level of symptoms tend to select the same response options (scalar invariance).
Models were estimated using methods appropriate for ordinal response scales (DWLS estimator), and we used White participants as the reference group.
Invariance at each level was supported when model fit did not meaningfully worsen upon adding constraints (ΔCFI < .010, ΔRMSEA < .015) 72 .
text.formatted: Invariance at each level was supported when model fit did not meaningfully worsen upon adding constraints (ΔCFI < .010, ΔRMSEA < .015) <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72</ref> .

text.text: Please see Table S1 for full results.
text.formatted: Please see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> for full results.

text.text: To test whether the association between specific word classes and internalizing symptoms differed across racial/ethnic groups, we quantified six psycholinguistic variables using LIWC-22 41 : first-person singular pronoun use (I-usage), negative sentiment (negative tone), positive sentiment (positive tone), first-person plural pronoun use (we-words), social language, and cognitive processing words.
text.formatted: To test whether the association between specific word classes and internalizing symptoms differed across racial/ethnic groups, we quantified six psycholinguistic variables using LIWC-22 <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41</ref> : first-person singular pronoun use (I-usage), negative sentiment (negative tone), positive sentiment (positive tone), first-person plural pronoun use (we-words), social language, and cognitive processing words.

text.text: I-usage, negative sentiment, and positive sentiment were the primary predictors of interest given prior evidence that all three vary across racial/ethnic groups and relate to internalizing symptoms 22, 25, 29 .
text.formatted: I-usage, negative sentiment, and positive sentiment were the primary predictors of interest given prior evidence that all three vary across racial/ethnic groups and relate to internalizing symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref> .

text.text: The remaining variables were examined as secondary analyses.

To test whether race/ethnicity moderated these associations, we estimated OLS regression models predicting baseline internalizing symptoms from each language feature, race/ethnicity, their interaction, and demographic covariates (age, sex at birth, education).
All continuous variables were standardized prior to modeling, and race/ethnicity was dummy-coded with White as the reference group.
Whenever this interaction was significant, we examined group-specific simple slopes and FDR-corrected 66 slope contrasts using the emtrends function from the emmeans package 73.
text.formatted: Whenever this interaction was significant, we examined group-specific simple slopes and FDR-corrected <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">66</ref> slope contrasts using the emtrends function from the emmeans package <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">73</ref>.

text.text: What linguistic patterns are associated with psychopathology across and within racial groups?
N-grams.
We extracted 1-3 word sequences (n-grams) from each group's responses using the topicsGrams function from the topics package in R 53 .
text.formatted: We extracted 1-3 word sequences (n-grams) from each group's responses using the topicsGrams function from the topics package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> .

text.text: In line with prior work 67, 74 , we applied three standard filters: n-grams had to 1) appear in at least 1% of responses, 2) have a pointwise mutual information (PMI) score > 3, and 3) fall within the top 5,000 n-grams per group.
text.formatted: In line with prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">67,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">74</ref> , we applied three standard filters: n-grams had to 1) appear in at least 1% of responses, 2) have a pointwise mutual information (PMI) score > 3, and 3) fall within the top 5,000 n-grams per group.

text.text: These filters ensure that retained n-grams were both common and linguistically coherent in our corpus.

Within each group, we built OLS regression models via the topicsTest function, regressing standardized internalizing symptoms onto each standardized n-gram usage frequency while controlling for demographic covariates.
We controlled for multiple comparisons using FDR-correction 66 within each racial/ethnic group.
text.formatted: We controlled for multiple comparisons using FDR-correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">66</ref> within each racial/ethnic group.

text.text: The extracted words and phrases were then classified into three groups: universal (significant associations in all four groups), shared (significant associations in two to three groups), or group-specific (significant associations in exactly one group).
For n-grams significant in more than one group, effect sizes were pooled using Fisher's z-transformation 75.
text.formatted: For n-grams significant in more than one group, effect sizes were pooled using Fisher's z-transformation <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">75</ref>.

text.text: We applied a pre-trained 2,000-topic Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model trained on Facebook status updates 42 , to assign each participant a probability score per topic (i.e., a cluster of words that reflect a semantic focus, like "shopping" or "parents") using the Differential Language Analysis ToolKit 76 .
text.formatted: We applied a pre-trained 2,000-topic Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model trained on Facebook status updates <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42</ref> , to assign each participant a probability score per topic (i.e., a cluster of words that reflect a semantic focus, like "shopping" or "parents") using the Differential Language Analysis ToolKit <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">76</ref> .

text.text: To restrict the number of tests we conducted (and avoid inflated error levels from testing 2,000 topics), we performed a multi-stage filtering process to exclude topics likely to be irrelevant to our research question.

First, we passed the list of words within each topic through LIWC and computed for each a composite score averaging standardized loadings across 28 relevant affective and social LIWC categories (e.g., negative emotion, anxiety, social behavior, health, etc.).
We excluded topics whose scores fell in the bottom 75% of these scores, leading to 500 topics that fell in the top quartile of affective and psychological language content.

Second, the first author manually reviewed this set and retained topics corresponding to clinically relevant constructs (e.g., emotional exhaustion, hopelessness, anhedonia, rumination, somatic symptoms, suicidality, panic, sleep disturbance, self-esteem, trauma).
Third, to ensure that we had not missed relevant topics in our first exclusion process, the first author re-reviewed all 2,000 topics and selected 32 additional topics that appeared to be relevant.
This resulted in a final candidate set of 54 topics.

For each of these 54 topics, we estimated OLS models predicting internalizing symptoms from topic usage, race/ethnicity, and their interaction; 2 topics survived FDR correction (p FDR < .05) and were carried forward for group-specific slope estimation and pairwise contrasts via emtrends and emmeans.
text.formatted: For each of these 54 topics, we estimated OLS models predicting internalizing symptoms from topic usage, race/ethnicity, and their interaction; 2 topics survived FDR correction (p FDR < .05) and were carried forward for group-specific slope estimation and pairwise contrasts via emtrends and emmeans.

text.text: Word embeddings.

To test whether machine learning models trained on open-ended language could predict internalizing symptoms, and critically whether predictive accuracy differed across racial/ethnic groups, we generated contextual word embeddings using MentalRoBERTa-base 54 , a 12-layer transformer language model fine-tuned on mental health text.
text.formatted: To test whether machine learning models trained on open-ended language could predict internalizing symptoms, and critically whether predictive accuracy differed across racial/ethnic groups, we generated contextual word embeddings using MentalRoBERTa-base <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> , a 12-layer transformer language model fine-tuned on mental health text.

text.text: Embeddings were extracted using the textEmbed function from the Text package in R 55 .
text.formatted: Embeddings were extracted using the textEmbed function from the Text package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: Following prior work 11, 44, 77 , we extracted the penultimate layer (11th layer) and mean-pooled across tokens to produce a single 768-dimension vector per participant.
text.formatted: Following prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">77</ref> , we extracted the penultimate layer (11th layer) and mean-pooled across tokens to produce a single 768-dimension vector per participant.

text.text: First we established whether MentalRoBERTa embeddings extracted from participants' open-ended responses could predict baseline internalizing symptoms across the full sample.
We trained a ridge regression model 78 on the full sample (N = 1,685) using the textTrainRegression function from the Text package in R 55 with cross-validation (5 outer folds).
text.formatted: We trained a ridge regression model <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">78</ref> on the full sample (N = 1,685) using the textTrainRegression function from the Text package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> with cross-validation (5 outer folds).

text.text: In each outer fold, 20% of data was held out as a test set; the remaining 80% was split into a training set (75%) and a validation set (25%) for penalty selection.
Ridge penalties (λ) ranging from 10⁻⁸ to 10⁸ were optimized via grid search minimizing RMSE on the validation set, with all splits stratified by outcome quartile.
We report one-tailed Pearson correlations between predicted and observed scores as our primary performance metric.
We then asked whether language-based prediction differed across racial/ethnic groups by training ridge regression models separately within each group.

Because each group's sample size fell below the number of embedding dimensions (N White = 412, N Black = 522, N Asian = 369, N Latino/Hispanic = 382; N parameters = 768), regularization must scale proportionally to the ratio of embedding dimensions to sample size 78 .
text.formatted: Because each group's sample size fell below the number of embedding dimensions (N White = 412, N Black = 522, N Asian = 369, N Latino/Hispanic = 382; N parameters = 768), regularization must scale proportionally to the ratio of embedding dimensions to sample size <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">78</ref> .

text.text: We therefore fixed the regularization penalty at λ = 250 for all group models.

Fixing λ uniformly across groups also enables direct comparison of the resulting coefficient vectors (β), as differences in β cannot be attributed to differences in regularization, an approach consistent with prior race-stratified language modeling work 29.
text.formatted: Fixing λ uniformly across groups also enables direct comparison of the resulting coefficient vectors (β), as differences in β cannot be attributed to differences in regularization, an approach consistent with prior race-stratified language modeling work <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29</ref>.

text.text: To test how well each group's model generalized when applied across-group to every other group, we computed a cross-group error difference for each participant.

This can be expressed as: dᵢ = |across-group errorᵢ| -|within-group errorᵢ|, where across-group errorᵢ is the error produced by the outside (applied) model on participant i, and in-group errorᵢ is the error produced by participant i's own group's dedicated model on that same participant.
Positive values indicate that a group's internalizing symptoms were predicted less accurately by a model trained on another group's data compared to its own group's model.
Negative values indicate the reverse.

We tested whether mean cross-group error differences differed from zero across the 12 model-group pairings using paired t-tests, with p-values FDR-corrected and confidence intervals constructed via bootstrapping (5,000 iterations with replacement).

We applied an identical procedure to test prospective generalization, training group-specific ridge regression models on Session 1 (baseline) language to predict Session 2 (follow-up) internalizing symptoms collected three weeks later (see Table S14 for results).
text.formatted: We applied an identical procedure to test prospective generalization, training group-specific ridge regression models on Session 1 (baseline) language to predict Session 2 (follow-up) internalizing symptoms collected three weeks later (see Table <ref type="table">S14</ref> for results).

text.text: To test whether language predicted follow-up symptoms beyond baseline severity, we additionally compared models including both baseline symptoms and language to see if they predicted follow-up symptoms beyond models including baseline symptoms alone (see Supplemental Information).
What do these machine learning models learn differently for each race?

Since a ridge regression model trained on embeddings learns a 768-dimensional coefficient vector (β) (i.e., a line of best fit) pointing from low-to high-severity language in embedding space, a participant's predicted severity score is simply their response's projection onto this vector.

This geometric structure affords a form of interpretability through projecting individual word embeddings onto the vector, by taking the dot product, allowing us to recover each word's contribution to severity predictions 43 .
text.formatted: This geometric structure affords a form of interpretability through projecting individual word embeddings onto the vector, by taking the dot product, allowing us to recover each word's contribution to severity predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> .

text.text: One can then construct a difference vector that represents differences in how words are weighted by each model simply by subtracting vectors for one ridge regression from the other 79 .
text.formatted: One can then construct a difference vector that represents differences in how words are weighted by each model simply by subtracting vectors for one ridge regression from the other <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">79</ref> .

text.text: Projecting words onto this difference vector then identifies words that are weighted differently across groups, revealing what each model has learned to treat as a marker of distress.

We exploited this property to characterize which words each group's model differentially weighted as indicators of symptom severity, revealing the extent to which racial/ethnic groups rely on distinct linguistic signals when expressing psychological distress, and whether systematic differences in these signals might relate to differences in cross-group prediction error.

Difference vectors were constructed by subtracting one group's L2-normalized β vector from another group's and renormalizing this difference vector (e.g., (β White -β Black ) / ||β White -β Black ||), so that positive projection scores indicate stronger association with severity in the first group's model and negative scores indicate the reverse.

We found that the White group's vector was the most geometrically distinctive of the four (mean pairwise cosine similarity to other groups' β vectors: 0.807, which is less than other racial groups' average similarity from each other: 0.847; Table S13).
text.formatted: We found that the White group's vector was the most geometrically distinctive of the four (mean pairwise cosine similarity to other groups' β vectors: 0.807, which is less than other racial groups' average similarity from each other: 0.847; Table <ref type="table">S13</ref>).

text.text: Thus, we constructed a summary contrast by subtracting the mean of the three minority β vectors from the White vector and renormalizing.
This yielded a single axis capturing the aggregate direction in which the White model's learned severity signal diverges from those of the minority group models.
We additionally computed difference vectors for each individual pairwise comparison (e.g., White vs.
Black, White vs.
Asian, White vs.
Latino/Hispanic); these are reported in the Supplemental Information (Figure S2) and showed patterns broadly consistent with the aggregate contrast reported here.
text.formatted: Latino/Hispanic); these are reported in the Supplemental Information (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S2</ref>) and showed patterns broadly consistent with the aggregate contrast reported here.

text.text: We compiled a list of all words used across participants, excluding common stopwords and words occurring less than 50 times, while retaining first-person pronouns throughout.

Morphological variants were collapsed via stemming with the most frequent surface form retained (e.g., "happier_", "happy;", "happiest"), embeddings were averaged to yield a single embedding per word type 55 .
text.formatted: Morphological variants were collapsed via stemming with the most frequent surface form retained (e.g., "happier_", "happy;", "happiest"), embeddings were averaged to yield a single embedding per word type <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: For each pairwise comparison, we used the union of both groups' word lists, averaging embeddings for words used by both groups.

We mean-centered word embeddings using the frequency-weighted corpus mean, so that projection scores reflect what is semantically distinctive about each word rather than its absolute position in embedding space.

We then projected each word onto the pairwise difference vectors described above, yielding a score that reflects how differently the two groups' models weight that word as a marker of symptom severity.

text.text: Because both our language variables and our outcome variable are related to symptom severity, this raised the possibility that the observed race-language interactions could partly reflect between-group differences in baseline severity rather than differences in the relationship between language and symptoms.
We used entropy balancing 39 to address this concern via the WeightIt R package 40 .
text.formatted: We used entropy balancing <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> to address this concern via the WeightIt R package <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> .

text.text: Briefly, entropy balancing is a reweighting procedure that assigns each participant a weight such that a specified covariate distribution is exactly equated across groups, while minimizing the exclusion of any participants.

This distinguishes it from other types of matching-based approaches (e.g., propensity score or nearest-neighbor matching), which achieve covariate balance by selectively excluding unmatched cases but can substantially reduce statistical power, particularly for smaller groups.

Among the (infinite) set of possible weights that would achieve exact balance on the target covariate, entropy balancing selects the set that remains maximally close to uniform weighting (i.e., minimizes the entropy distance from a weight of 1 for every participant), which prevents the reweighted estimates from being driven disproportionately by a small number of extreme-weighted individuals.
We specified that the model should balance all four racial/ethnic groups to the pooled mean of baseline internalizing severity across the sample.
This produced exact mean balance across groups (standardized mean difference = 0; weighted M = 12.82 for all groups) and near-exact variance balance (variance ratio = 1.12).

Weights ranged from 2.84 to 5.15 (M = 4.00), and effective sample sizes were retained at 98.0-99.9% of the unweighted N in every group (White: 411/412; Black: 514/522; Asian: 369/369; Latino/Hispanic: 375/382).

We then reran our primary race/ethnicity-language interaction models predicting internalizing severity from the interaction of race/ethnicity and each of the LIWC language variables (I-usage, positive tone, and negative tone) with significant interactions, covarying age, sex, and education on the entropy-balanced sample.
We used weighted regression with bootstrapped standard errors (R = 5,000 replications) to account for the additional estimation uncertainty introduced by the weights themselves.

Because bootstrapped/sandwich variance-covariance matrices do not support a classical F-test with well-defined denominator degrees of freedom, omnibus interaction tests are reported as Wald χ² statistics.

All three race/ethnicity-language interactions remained significant following severity balancing and FDR correction: I-usage, χ²(3) = 9.89, p FDR = .029; negative tone, χ²(3) = 8.31, p FDR = .040; positive tone, χ²(3) = 10.18, p FDR = .029.
We additionally examined FDR-corrected pairwise contrasts for each interaction to identify which specific group comparisons were driving each omnibus effect (Table S4).
text.formatted: We additionally examined FDR-corrected pairwise contrasts for each interaction to identify which specific group comparisons were driving each omnibus effect (Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: The I-usage interaction retained individually significant pairwise contrasts as reported in the full sample: White participants' I-usage slope differed significantly from both Black (p FDR = .032) and Latino/Hispanic (p FDR = .032) participants' slopes, closely replicating the pattern observed in the unweighted analysis.

Neither tone variable retained significant pairwise contrasts after correction (all ps > .11; Table S4), but the omnibus interaction remained significant and the direction of differences were the same: For negative tone, the Latino/Hispanic slope was stronger than all others, and for positive tone, the Asian slope was stronger than all others (See Table S3).

text.text: We Words.
We-word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between We-word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.32, p = .267).
Slopes for each group were small and directionally inconsistent (see Tables S7-S8; See Figure S1a).
text.formatted: Slopes for each group were small and directionally inconsistent (see Tables <ref type="table">S7-S8</ref>; See Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S1a</ref>).

text.text: We-word usage thus does not appear to be a reliable marker of internalizing distress in this sample, regardless of racial/ethnic group.
Social word usage did not significantly predict internalizing symptoms in any group, and there was no significant interaction between social word use and race/ethnicity (F(3, 1662) = 1.40, p = .243).
Slopes for each group were small and directionally inconsistent (see Tables S7-S8; see Figure S1b).
text.formatted: Slopes for each group were small and directionally inconsistent (see Tables <ref type="table">S7-S8</ref>; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S1b</ref>).

text.text: Social word usage thus does not appear to be a reliable marker of internalizing distress in this sample, regardless of racial/ethnic group.

The Cognitive Processing × race/ethnicity interaction term was not significant (F(3, 1662) = 0.22, p = .886), indicating no reliable evidence that the association between cognitive processing word usage and internalizing symptoms differs by race/ethnicity.

Nonetheless, in post-hoc group-level tests, the confidence interval for Black participants excluded zero, though this effect did not survive FDR correction (p FDR = .188; see Table S7; see Figure S1c).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, in post-hoc group-level tests, the confidence interval for Black participants excluded zero, though this effect did not survive FDR correction (p FDR = .188; see Table <ref type="table">S7</ref>; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">S1c</ref>).

text.text: No other group showed evidence of an effect with slopes that were positive and similar in magnitude across all four groups.

Given the null omnibus interaction and the failure of the Black group effect to survive correction, cognitive processing word usage does not appear to be a reliable marker of internalizing distress in this sample, and there is no evidence that its relationship with symptoms varies by race/ethnicity.

text.text: To complement the machine learning analyses reported in the main text, we examined pairwise cosine similarities between the group-specific model coefficient vectors.
This provided us with a direct measure of how similarly each racial/ethnic group's model weights language features (in this case word embeddings) when predicting symptoms.

text.text: Contrast Vector Visualization.
Each panel shows one pairwise comparison between two race/ethnicity groups' learned β vectors, labeled by panel title (e.g., "White vs.
Black").

Within a panel, a word's position reflects how differently the two named groups' models associate that word with internalizing symptom severity: positive values indicate the first-named group's model links the word more strongly to high severity than the second-named group's model does; negative values indicate the reverse.
Bar color identifies which of the two groups' models weights the word more heavily toward severity, following the four-group color scheme used throughout (White, Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic).

The x-axis reflects how much more strongly one model weights that word toward severity than the other, with larger absolute values indicating greater disagreement in how strongly the word signals severity.
Panels show the top and bottom 15 words drawn from the union vocabulary of the two compared groups (minimum word frequency = 50).
All group-specific models were fitted with matched hyperparameters (fixed λ = 250) so that differences reflect group differences in language rather than differences in model regularization.
Having established that language-based markers of internalizing severity differ across racial/ethnic groups at baseline, we next asked whether these differences have prospective implications.
That is, whether the same baseline language features that track concurrent symptom severity also predict symptom levels three weeks later, and whether that predictive signal varies by race/ethnicity.
Of the 1,685 participants who completed baseline measures, 1,465 (86.9%) completed the follow-up survey approximately three weeks later, yielding an attrition rate of 13.1% (N = 220).

Retention rates differed significantly across racial/ethnic groups (χ²(3) = 15.60, p = .001): White participants had the highest retention (92.0%), followed by Black (87.4%), Asian (84.3%), and Latino/Hispanic (83.5%) participants.

To characterize differential attrition, we estimated a single logistic regression model predicting follow-up completion from baseline internalizing severity, race/ethnicity, age, sex, and education level.

Neither baseline internalizing severity (OR = 0.99, 95% CI [0.98, 1.00], p = .14), age (OR = 1.07, 95% CI [0.92, 1.25], p = .364), sex (all p > .13), nor education level (all p > .12) significantly predicted follow-up completion, indicating that attrition was unrelated to symptom severity or these demographic factors.
text.formatted: Neither baseline internalizing severity (OR = 0.99, 95% CI [0.98, 1.00], p = .14), age (OR = 1.07, 95% CI [0.92, 1.25], p = .364), sex (all p > .13), nor education level (all p > .12) significantly predicted follow-up completion, indicating that attrition was unrelated to symptom severity or these demographic factors.

text.text: FDR-corrected pairwise contrasts on race/ethnicity indicated that White participants were significantly more likely to complete Session 2 than Asian (OR = 2.07, 95% CI [1.10, 3.89], p = .007) and Latino/Hispanic participants (OR = 2.20, 95% CI [1.19, 4.07], p = .004); the White-Black contrast did not survive correction (OR = 1.62, 95% CI [0.89, 2.94], p = .068).
No other pairwise group differences were significant (all p FDR > .17).
text.formatted: No other pairwise group differences were significant (all p FDR > .17).

text.text: All primary analyses are reported for the full baseline sample (N = 1,685); follow-up analyses presented in the supplement are based on the 1,465 participants with complete longitudinal data.

We re-estimated each moderation model with follow-up internalizing symptoms as the outcome, controlling for baseline symptoms and demographics, to isolate the prospective signal in language beyond symptom stability.

Repeating these analyses on follow-up data showed that no LIWC language feature showed a significant race moderation when controlling for baseline symptoms: I-usage (F(3, 1441) = 0.26, p = .856), negative tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.89, p = .444), positive tone (F(3, 1441) = 0.69, p = .557), we-words (F(3, 1441) = 0.58, p = .630), social words (F(3, 1441) = 0.53, p = .661), and cognitive processing words (F(3, 1441) = 1.75, p = .155).
Importantly, we in fact observed that group-level slopes were uniformly small and none survived FDR correction (p FDR > .05).
text.formatted: Importantly, we in fact observed that group-level slopes were uniformly small and none survived FDR correction (p FDR > .05).

text.text: These null results indicate that (i) LIWC language features captured at Session 1 (baseline) do not predict follow-up ratings after controlling for baseline symptoms, and (ii) no LIWC language features differentially predict symptom change depending on one's racial/ethnic group.
We conducted a series of follow-up tests to investigate why we found no prospective symptom prediction using LIWC variables.
These analyses showed that internalizing symptoms were highly stable across the 3-week interval between sessions.
Session 1 and Session 2 scores were very strongly correlated (r = .817, 95% CI [.799, .833], p < .001), indicating that individual differences in symptom severity were largely preserved over time.

text.text: The models above provide evidence that language shows differential prediction of symptoms beyond the current timepoint, but because they do not control for baseline symptoms (as the LIWC analyses did), they do not show that language can predict changes in symptoms beyond baseline levels.
Following recent recommendations for evaluating prospective prediction 80 , we next tested whether language improved prediction beyond what baseline symptoms alone could achieve.
text.formatted: Following recent recommendations for evaluating prospective prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">80</ref> , we next tested whether language improved prediction beyond what baseline symptoms alone could achieve.

text.text: We first performed this comparison in the pooled sample of all participants who completed follow-up (N = 1,465), comparing a model that predicted follow-up symptoms from baseline symptoms alone to one that used both baseline symptoms and participants' language.

As with the other pooled models, the penalty was selected through cross-validation, so we fit this model with the text package, entering baseline symptoms as an additional predictor alongside the language embeddings.
We then performed the same comparison within each group.
Both models were tested on the same cross-validation splits.

In the combined group-specific models, language was regularized with the same fixed penalty used throughout the paper (λ = 250), but baseline symptoms were left unpenalized so the model could use them in full.
Because the text package does not allow a single predictor to go unpenalized, we fit these group-specific models with glmnett 81 .
text.formatted: Because the text package does not allow a single predictor to go unpenalized, we fit these group-specific models with glmnett <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">81</ref> .

text.text: We then tested whether adding language reduced prediction error (paired t-tests on each participant's absolute error) and how much it changed accuracy (the difference in correlations, Δr, with 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals).
P-values for the group-specific models were corrected for multiple comparisons across the four groups.
Adding language did not improve prediction of follow-up symptoms beyond baseline symptoms (Table S15).
text.formatted: Adding language did not improve prediction of follow-up symptoms beyond baseline symptoms (Table <ref type="table">S15</ref>).

text.text: In the pooled sample, adding language to baseline symptoms slightly reduced accuracy (r = .761 vs. .816; Δr = -.055, 95% CI [-.069, -.041]; t(1464) = -10.9, p < .001).
text.formatted: In the pooled sample, adding language to baseline symptoms slightly reduced accuracy (r = .761 vs. .816; Δr = -.055, 95% CI [-.069, -.041]; t(1464) = -10.9, p < .001).

text.text: Within groups, combined models (i.e., baseline symptoms and language) performed nearly identically to baseline-only models: White (r = .766 vs. .760; Δr = .005, 95% CI [-.004, .015], p FDR = .66), Black (r = .824 vs. .823; Δr = .001, 95% CI [-.003, .006], p FDR = .99), Latino/Hispanic (r = .825 vs. .827; Δr = -.002, 95% CI [-.009, .005], p FDR = .66), and Asian (r = .845 vs. .846; Δr = -.001, 95% CI [-.006, .003], p FDR = .99).
We also tested whether the prospective cross-group differences reported above reflected language once baseline symptoms were controlled.

For each of the 12 model-group pairings, we computed the cross-group error differential (dᵢ) for the combined models and subtracted the same quantity from the baseline-only models, isolating the portion attributable to language.
None were significant (all p FDR ≥ .85; Table S16).
text.formatted: None were significant (all p FDR ≥ .85; Table <ref type="table">S16</ref>).

text.text: Together, these results indicate that the prospective predictions reported above do not survive when baseline symptom severity is controlled for.
Group differences in the accuracy of language-based estimates persist to symptom reports three weeks later, but language did not predict change in symptoms beyond baseline, for any group.

S1 to S3 Tables S1 to S16 Measurement Invariance Prior to primary analyses, we tested measurement invariance of the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 across racial/ethnic groups using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA).
text.formatted: Author notes: *Correspondence should be addressed to Steven Mesquiti (email: sm9518@princeton.edu) This file includes: Supplementary text Figs. <ref type="table">S1 to S3</ref> Tables <ref type="table">S1 to S16</ref> Measurement Invariance Prior to primary analyses, we tested measurement invariance of the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 across racial/ethnic groups using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis (MGCFA).

text.text: We specified a unidimensional factor structure for each scale and estimated three progressively constrained models: configural invariance (same factor structure across groups, all parameters freely estimated), metric invariance (factor loadings additionally constrained to equality across groups), and scalar invariance (item thresholds additionally constrained to equality across groups).
All models were estimated using the diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS) estimator with ordered categorical indicators, appropriate for ordinal Likert-type items.
Invariance was evaluated using changes in CFI and RMSEA between nested models 72 .
text.formatted: Invariance was evaluated using changes in CFI and RMSEA between nested models <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">72</ref> .

text.text: White participants served as the reference group throughout.
Both scales demonstrated full scalar invariance across all four racial/ethnic groups.

For the PHQ-8, CFI remained stable across metric (CFI = .998, ΔCFI = .0001) and scalar (CFI = .998, ΔCFI = .0003) constraints, with RMSEA improving monotonically from configural to scalar (.063 → .058 → .048), indicating that the successive equality constraints stabilized rather than degraded model fit.

For the GAD-7, fit indices were similarly stable across metric (CFI = .999, ΔCFI = .0001) and scalar (CFI = .999, ΔCFI = .0004) constraints, with RMSEA again improving from configural to scalar (.063 → .060 → .041).

Taken together, these results affirm that the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 measure their respective constructs equivalently across racial/ethnic groups at the scale level, supporting the validity of group mean comparisons.

text.text: Robustness Check Group differences in internalizing symptoms.
To test whether our racial/ethnic groups differed in symptom severity, we conducted a one-way ANOVA.

We observed that racial/ethnic groups in our sample differed in mean baseline internalizing severity (PHQ-8 + GAD-7 composite; White M = 13.2, SD = 11.5; Black M = 11.4, SD = 11.4; Asian M = 12.6, SD = 11.7; Latino/Hispanic M = 14.5, SD = 12.65, F(3, 1681) = 5.52, p < .001).
text.formatted: We observed that racial/ethnic groups in our sample differed in mean baseline internalizing severity (PHQ-8 + GAD-7 composite; White M = 13.2, SD = 11.5; Black M = 11.4, SD = 11.4; Asian M = 12.6, SD = 11.7; Latino/Hispanic M = 14.5, SD = 12.65, F(3, 1681) = 5.52, p < .001).

text.text: Tukey HSD-adjusted pairwise comparisons revealed that this effect was driven primarily by Latino/Hispanic participants, who reported significantly higher internalizing symptoms than Black participants (p < .001).
text.formatted: Tukey HSD-adjusted pairwise comparisons revealed that this effect was driven primarily by Latino/Hispanic participants, who reported significantly higher internalizing symptoms than Black participants (p < .001).

text.text: No other pairwise comparisons reached significance (all p's > .07; see Table S2), including the Latino/Hispanic-Asian contrast, which showed a similar-sized gap but did not survive correction.
text.formatted: No other pairwise comparisons reached significance (all p's > .07; see Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>), including the Latino/Hispanic-Asian contrast, which showed a similar-sized gap but did not survive correction.

text.text: Internalizing Symptom Pairwise Comparisons Across Race/Ethnicity point on average (M CHANGE = 0.82, SD CHANGE = 6.93, M PRE = 12.64, SD PRE = 11.76; M FU = 11.83, SD FU = 11.05).

Taken together, these results indicate that internalizing symptoms remained largely stable across the 3-week interval, leaving comparatively little within-person variance for Session-1 language features to predict at follow-up.

To test whether Session 1 (baseline) language predicted follow-up internalizing symptoms 3 weeks later, we estimated a parallel set of ridge regression models using the same architecture and hyperparameters described above.

A pooled prospective model was trained on the follow-up sample (N = 1,465) using 5-fold cross-validation with penalty selection via grid search (as described for the baseline models); group-specific prospective models used the fixed penalty of λ = 250.

All prospective models used Session 1 language embeddings as predictors and Session 2 internalizing symptoms as the outcome, with no baseline symptom covariate included in the machine learning models themselves (models controlling for baseline symptoms are reported below).
The pooled model demonstrated moderate accuracy predicting follow-up symptoms from baseline language (r = 0.565, 95%CI [0.535, 1], p < .001).
text.formatted: The pooled model demonstrated moderate accuracy predicting follow-up symptoms from baseline language (r = 0.565, 95%CI [0.535, 1], p < .001).

text.text: Within-group models showed comparable prospective validity across groups: White (r = 0.470, 95%CI [0.401, 1]), Black (r = 0.506, 95%CI [0.447, 1]), Latino/Hispanic (r = 0.619, 95%CI [0.559, 1]), and Asian (r = 0.594, 95%CI [0.530, 1]; all p's < .001).
text.formatted: Within-group models showed comparable prospective validity across groups: White (r = 0.470, 95%CI [0.401, 1]), Black (r = 0.506, 95%CI [0.447, 1]), Latino/Hispanic (r = 0.619, 95%CI [0.559, 1]), and Asian (r = 0.594, 95%CI [0.530, 1]; all p's < .001).

text.text: A one-way ANOVA revealed no significant differences in absolute prediction errors across racial/ethnic groups (F(3, 1461) = 1.775, p = .150) indicating comparable prospective model performance across groups.
Without controlling for baseline symptoms, cross-group generalization revealed a pattern mirroring the findings for concurrent models.

The White-trained model again produced significantly higher across-group error when applied to Latino/Hispanic (p FDR = .001), Asian (p FDR < .001), and Black participants (p FDR = .029) (see Table S14 for full statistics).
text.formatted: The White-trained model again produced significantly higher across-group error when applied to Latino/Hispanic (p FDR = .001), Asian (p FDR < .001), and Black participants (p FDR = .029) (see Table <ref type="table">S14</ref> for full statistics).

text.text: Again, the Black-trained model generalized significantly poorly to Asian participants (p FDR = .027), and the Asian-trained model produced significantly lower across-group error on White participants (p FDR = .029).
As for the baseline model, across all 12 pairings, the White model remained the only model to produce significantly higher errors on all three out-group comparisons (see Figure S3; see Table S14).
